description: Vigía Orbital: Desde el espacio, cuidamos nuestra tierra. Mapa interactivo de incendios en Costa Rica (2012-2025) con datos MODIS y VIIRS de la NASA, correlacionados con sequía, temperatura y lluvia. ¿Por qué 2024 tuvo el doble de incendios? Ya tenemos IA/ML, desarrollo web y visualización de datos. Buscamos 1-2 personas: geociencias y teledetección (geografía, geología, meteorología, ambiental, forestal, SIG) y gestión de riesgos con habilidad para presentar. Español o inglés.
summary: Vigía Orbital introduces the Risk of Fire Index, a new index produced by a machine learning model built on NASA data that forecasts wildfire risk 5 days ahead for the 11 cantons of Guanacaste, Costa Rica: a weather forecast, but for fires. For each canton and day, the index gives the probability that satellites detect a vegetation fire, a level (Low, Moderate, High, Very high, Extreme) and the reasons behind it. To build it I first harmonized NASA's MODIS and VIIRS hot spot records (four satellites, 2012–2026) into one consistent measure: one reference satellite per period and fire days per canton, instead of raw detection counts that jump every time a satellite is added. On that record I trained the model (see the Colab notebook): one logistic regression for each forecast day (1 to 5 days ahead) that starts from the normal risk for each canton and week and adjusts it with current weather (NASA POWER), vegetation dryness (MODIS NDVI and NDMI), recent fire (NASA FIRMS) and terrain (NASADEM). Tested blind, season by season from 2013 to 2025, it is 8.4 % more accurate than an average year and better in 12 of 14 seasons. The index is also available through a website and an open API, including a text message under 1 KB for brigades with weak signal. Guanacaste holds 63 % of Costa Rica's fire detections, so five days of warning helps crews be in the right place before the fire.
details:
What it is. The project is the Risk of Fire Index: a machine learning model built on NASA data that, for each canton of Guanacaste and each of the next five days, gives the probability that satellites detect a vegetation fire, with a level (Low, Moderate, High, Very high, Extreme) and the reasons behind it. The website, the API and the notebook demonstrate how to use the index and how it is built:

- Live website: https://lg061870.github.io/vigia-orbital/ (pick a canton and a day; turn back the clock to any date since 2012 and compare the forecast with what the satellites detected)

- Open API: https://lg061870-vigia-orbital-api.hf.space/api/docs (forecast on request, also as a plain text message)

- Reproducible notebook: https://colab.research.google.com/github/lg061870/vigia-orbital/blob/main/notebooks/vigia_orbital_modelo.ipynb

How it addresses the challenge (harmonization). VIIRS (375 m) detects 3.5 to 5.4 times more fires than MODIS (1 km), and the ratio changes by year and canton, so no single conversion factor works. Each new satellite also inflates raw counts. My harmonized measure uses one reference satellite per period (VIIRS S-NPP for 2012–2025, NOAA-20 from 2026), keeps vegetation fires only, converts UTC to local dates, and counts fire days per canton (yes/no). I checked the hand-over: NOAA-21 matches S-NPP within ±4 % per year (2023–2025), so the record continues after S-NPP.

How the model works. One logistic regression per day ahead (1 to 5). It starts from history (the normal for that canton and week of the year, 2012–2025) and adjusts for weather compared with normal (days without rain, maximum temperature, wind, humidity, soil wetness, 30-day rain), vegetation compared with normal (NDVI, NDMI), recent fire in the canton (last 7 days) and terrain. Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood.

Validation. Leave-one-season-out, 2013–2025: each season is forecast by a model that never saw it. Brier skill score +8.4 % against the canton-and-week climatology; AUC 0.932 against 0.919; positive in 12 of 14 seasons (up to +21 % in the worst seasons); when it forecasts 90 % or more, fire is observed 96 % of the time (7,900 canton-days); skill from +7.8 % on day 1 to +5.4 % on day 5. On the 2026 season, a true out-of-sample test, it tied with climatology.

Benefits. SINAC's fire program and brigades can decide where to position crews for the next five days; firefighters and the national emergency commission can decide when to scale up or stand down; municipalities can time prevention messages and burn controls.

Limits. A light rain can make it too optimistic for a few days; MODIS vegetation products arrive weeks late; it works at canton level; "fire" means a satellite detection, so small fires and fires under clouds are missed; it has not yet been validated against SINAC field reports.

Tools. Python, pandas, NumPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, GeoPandas, rasterio, DuckDB, Google Colab, FastAPI, Leaflet, GitHub Pages and Actions, Hugging Face Spaces.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS: MODIS (Terra/Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) active fire / hot spot detections
NASA POWER: daily weather (temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation, soil wetness)
NASA MODIS vegetation and surface reflectance products MOD13Q1 / MYD13Q1 (NDVI, NBR) and MOD09A1 / MYD09A1 (NDMI), v061
NASA GIBS / Worldview: satellite imagery shown on the website and slides
NASA ARSET: training \"Using the Fire Mapping Tools to Map Fires\" (reference for the manual workflow)
projectRefs: NOAA Climate Prediction Center: Oceanic Niño Index (ONI)
Microsoft Planetary Computer: access to MODIS products
Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX): OpenStreetMap, Kontur, UNFPA layers
